Let us take up the former voice and seize a prophetic breast, for it still has milk and good visions. For it says, 'Rejoice, daughter of Zion; cry out, daughter of Jerusalem.' And why 'daughter of Zion' and not Zion, and 'daughter of Jerusalem' and not Jerusalem? Pay attention carefully, I beg. Just as the names of plants and birds and quadrupeds and humans have differences in form and power, so also each horn of the divine sayings has its own power and vision. Let us investigate why the prophet first calls the faithful Jerusalem 'daughter of Zion' and then 'daughter of Jerusalem.' It says, 'Rejoice, daughter of Zion; cry out, daughter of Jerusalem.' Zion is interpreted as 'thirsty'; and this is the synagogue of the righteous and prophets, who from eternity until the coming of Christ thirsted to be united and pleasing to the divine and worshipful substance of the deity, as the chief of the apostles Peter says: 'So that they may become partakers of the divine nature.' These, seeking the Lord and thirsting, were called Zion, as one of them said: 'My soul thirsted for the strong living God.' When they attained and drew near, or rather appeared and saw his face, they became Jerusalem, 'seeing God and the watchtower of all knowledge.'

The daughter of Zion calls the faithful in the Lord, those thirsting through faith and seeking through the work of the gospel's commandments to find the Lord, the one hidden in them, as the Holy Spirit says. This is the generation seeking the Lord, seeking the face of the God of Jacob. When they attain, they are called the daughter of the aforementioned Jerusalem, beholding God and contemplating spiritual knowledge. The prophet, exhorting God through the Spirit, says to show this Zion and Jerusalem, saying: 'Remember your assembly, which you acquired from the beginning.' Then, with the mother, Zion, 'Rejoice, daughter of Zion; proclaim, daughter of Jerusalem', crying out heavenly with the mother. 'Hosanna in the highest, blessed is the one coming in the name of the Lord.' The gospel says: 'When they approached Jerusalem and came to Bethphage'. Jesus sent two of his disciples, who are two groups of prophets and apostles, to the mount of Olives, which is the faithful church from the people.

For he sent them to all the inhabited world of the nations, because they were previously opposed to the faithful church from the people. For at a suitable time he sent them to the village opposite of the nations. For it was ready to receive the previously mentioned two choirs of apostles and prophets. And to bring to him the colt, which are the nations, to mount and reign over them, as the psalmist says. He reigns over the nations, the Lord sits on his holy throne. On which no human has ever sat. For neither is God mounting and reigning over them, nor law nor prophets. Having loosed him, he says, bring him to me. For the apostles loosed the nations from darkness, that is, from ignorance of God, from error, from sin, from foreign slavery, from the power of darkness, from the ruler of this age. And they brought them to their creator and lord. And behold, he sits on them and reigns as on the cherubim, crying out and saying. Hosanna in the highest, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. Peace on earth and glory in the highest. For Luke says so. Peace on earth, why does he say this? Did the angels not have peace on earth? Yes, and they had peace within themselves, the peace that surpasses all understanding, as the wise Paul says. They had peace in heaven, but not with humans. pass_b_english: Let us take up the former voice once more and seize a prophetic breast, for it still has milk and good visions.
For it says, 'Rejoice exceedingly, daughter of Zion; cry out, daughter of Jerusalem'.

The prophet cries out with this distinction, and we must pay close attention to it, because the names of plants, birds, quadrupeds, and humans all have different forms and powers, and similarly, each horn of the divine sayings has its own unique power and vision.
We need to investigate why the prophet first calls the faithful Jerusalem 'daughter of Zion' and then 'daughter of Jerusalem'.

The answer lies in the meaning of Zion, which is interpreted as 'thirsty', referring to the synagogue of the righteous and prophets who, the prophets, who from eternity until the coming of Christ thirsted to be united and pleasing to the divine and worshipful substance of the deity, as the chief of the apostles Peter says, 'So that they may become partakers of the divine nature'.

These individuals, who sought the Lord and thirsted for Him, were called Zion, and when they finally attained their goal and saw God's face, they became Jerusalem, the city that sees God and is the watchtower of all knowledge.

The daughter of Zion calls the faithful in the Lord, those who thirst through faith and seek through the work of the gospel's commandments to find the Lord, the one hidden in them, as the Holy Spirit says, 'This is the generation that seeks the Lord, seeking the face of the God of Jacob'.
When they attain their goal, they are called the daughter of the aforementioned Jerusalem, for they behold God and contemplate spiritual knowledge.
The prophet, exhorting God through the Spirit, asks Him to reveal this Zion and Jerusalem, saying, 'Remember your assembly, which you acquired from the beginning'.

Then, crying out with the mother, Zion, 'Rejoice exceedingly, daughter of Zion; proclaim, daughter of Jerusalem', they cry out heavenly, 'Hosanna in the highest, blessed is the one coming in the name of the Lord'.
The gospel says, 'When they approached Jerusalem and came to Bethphage'.
Jesus sent two of his disciples, who are two groups of prophets and apostles, to the mount of Olives, which is the faithful church from the people.
For he sent them to all the inhabited world of the nations, because they were previously opposed to the faithful church from the people.
For at a suitable time he sent them to the village opposite of the nations. For it was ready to receive the previously mentioned two choirs of apostles and prophets.
And to bring to him the colt, which are the nations, to mount and reign over them, as the psalmist says, 'The Lord reigns over the nations, the Lord sits on his holy throne'.
On which no human has ever sat. For neither is God mounting and reigning over them, nor law nor prophets.

Having loosed him, he says, bring him to me. For the apostles loosed the nations from darkness, that is, from ignorance of God, from error, from sin, from foreign slavery, from the power of darkness, from the ruler of this age. And they brought them to their creator and lord.
And behold, he sits on them and reigns as on the cherubim, crying out and saying, 'Hosanna in the highest, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord'.

Peace on earth and glory in the highest. For Luke says so. Peace on earth, why does he say this? Did the angels not have peace on earth? Yes, and they had peace within themselves, the peace that surpasses all understanding, as the wise Paul says. They had peace in heaven, but not with humans. The heaven had peace in itself.
When the angels saw this, …
The prophet says, 'Rejoice exceedingly, daughter of Zion; cry out, daughter of Jerusalem', and this is a call to the faithful to rejoice and cry out, for the Lord is coming.
The gospel says, 'When they approached Jerusalem and came to Bethphage', and this is a fulfillment of the prophecy.
And Jesus sent two of his disciples to the mount of Olives, which is the faithful church from the people, to bring to him the colt, which are the nations, so that he could mount and reign over them.
And the psalmist says, 'The Lord reigns over the nations, the Lord sits on his holy throne', and this is a declaration of the Lord's reign over the nations.

And the apostles loosed the nations from darkness, and brought them to their creator and lord, and behold, he sits on them and reigns as on the cherubim, crying out and saying, 'Hosanna in the highest, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord'.
And then it says, 'Peace on earth and glory in the highest', and this is a declaration of peace and glory.
And when the angels saw this, they had peace within themselves, but not with humans, and the heaven had peace in itself, and then they said…
